summary:
All eight named works exist and were verified against arXiv primary sources (abstracts read verbatim; experiment/limitations sections fetched where the protocol question was load-bearing). The advisor's assertion holds: each of "retargeting helps tracking", "physics feedback into retargeting", and "shared morphology conditioning" is independently and recently claimed, by multiple papers each, and none is defensible novelty alone.

The decisive finding is that NOT ONE of the eight evaluates on a held-out ROBOT. Every single one generalizes only over held-out MOTIONS. The three cross-embodiment papers (AdaMorph, G-DReaM, X-Morph) are structurally unable to do zero-shot held-out-robot inference: AdaMorph learns a per-robot prompt bank AND a per-robot output MLP head (a new robot has neither), G-DReaM requires ~5h/30k-step retraining with the new skeleton added to the training set, and X-Morph trains per source-target pair. The three physics-feedback papers (ReActor, OmniTrack, NMR) are explicitly per-robot: ReActor re-runs ~6h of bilevel RL per embodiment; OmniTrack's references ARE that robot's own policy rollouts; NMR states in its own limitations that "CEPR is morphology-specific; extending to other platforms requires regenerating the data pipeline, and developing morphology-conditioned architectures remains a direction for future work." That sentence is the literature naming the gap the hypothesis targets.

The four-way conjunction (transferable correction learning + strict held-out-robot protocol + preserved human intent + downstream learning benefit) is UNCLAIMED. But it is unclaimed as a conjunction only — every conjunct has a strong 2026 owner, and no single conjunct survives as the contribution. The paper is therefore not "a new method"; it is "a new claim about transfer", and it lives or dies on the leave-one-robot-out protocol plus a scaling-in-number-of-training-robots curve. Two threats are sharper than the eight listed: X-Morph (arXiv:2606.30290) already combines spec conditioning + physics-aware correction + closed-loop tracking and only stops short of held-out-robot transfer, and H-Zero (arXiv:2512.00971) already normalizes leave-one-robot-out with embodiment descriptors for locomotion policies — so a reviewer will call the protocol standard practice, not contribution.

findings.claim: GMR studies retargeting artifacts affecting downstream tracking, and does so across robots
findings.evidence: arXiv:2510.02252 (ICRA 2026), Araújo, Ze, Xu, Wu, Liu. Abstract: 'we systematically evaluate how retargeting quality affects policy performance when excessive reward tuning is suppressed'. Experiments: 'We retarget each motion sequence to a Unitree G1 robot.' Limitations: 'Another limitation is that we only consider the Unitree G1.' Protocol: 'we use BeyondMimic for training and evaluation of RL policies... BeyondMimic does not depend on reward tuning and is developed independently from the retargeting methods we use, making it a fair method to evaluate them.'
findings.consequence: GMR owns the causal claim 'retargeting quality -> tracker robustness' and owns the clean confound-free protocol (independent, reward-tuning-free tracker). It does NOT own cross-robot anything: single robot, pure IK/optimization (5 steps: key-body matching, pose alignment, non-uniform local scaling, IK with rotation constraints, fine-tuning), zero learned components. Adopt its BeyondMimic-style isolation protocol verbatim or a reviewer will attribute your gains to reward tuning.

findings.claim: NMR learns retargeting corrections from physics refinement and improves downstream policy convergence
findings.evidence: arXiv:2603.22201, 'Make Tracking Easy: Neural Motion Retargeting for Humanoid Whole-body Control'. Abstract: 'NMR-generated references accelerate the convergence of downstream whole-body control policies'. Robots: Unitree G1 only. Convergence metric: 'Policies trained on NMR references reach longer episodes and higher rewards' (training curves vs GMR, PHUMA, NMR w/o RL; no epochs-to-convergence number). Limitations, verbatim: 'CEPR is morphology-specific; extending to other platforms requires regenerating the data pipeline, and developing morphology-conditioned architectures remains a direction for future work.'
findings.consequence: This is simultaneously the biggest threat and the strongest license. It already owns 'learned correction + physics-derived supervision + downstream convergence benefit' — three of your four conjuncts, minus transfer. But its own limitations sentence names morphology-conditioned architectures as future work. Cite that sentence in your intro; it converts your contribution from 'combination' into 'answering a stated open question'. Note the correction is learned from OFFLINE RL-expert data repair, not from the closed loop of the tracker you are trying to help — that distinction is thin and a reviewer may not grant it.

findings.claim: ReActor couples retargeting-parameter adaptation with tracking-policy learning, and this constitutes prior art for physics feedback
findings.evidence: arXiv:2605.06593, also ACM TOG (doi 10.1145/3811378), authors incl. Ruben Grandia. Abstract: 'a bilevel optimization framework that jointly adapts reference motions to a robot's morphology while training a tracking policy using reinforcement learning'. Upper level = retargeting parameters p (bounded position/orientation offsets, delta_pos/delta_ori <= 0.5); lower level = RL tracking policy. Embodiments: Unitree G1 (29 DoF), a ~0.84m 20-DoF humanoid, ANYmal D quadruped. Requires '20k iterations (~6 h)' of RL per target robot; generalization tested only on unseen motions within the same robot. Downstream: 97.45% SR on G1 vs OmniRetarget 95.51%, GMR 89.93%.
findings.consequence: Physics-in-the-loop retargeting is fully claimed, on three embodiments including a quadruped, with hardware validation and a downstream-tracking win over GMR and OmniRetarget. Your 'closed-loop tracking experience' conjunct is dead on its own. What ReActor cannot do: amortize. It solves a low-dimensional parameter vector per robot at ~6 GPU-hours each, learns nothing reusable, and never transfers. Your compute-matched comparison MUST be against ReActor on the held-out robot, or the obvious rebuttal is 'just run ReActor for 6 hours on the new robot'. Lower confidence on the second humanoid's name (rendered as 'Lima' in the HTML fetch; PDF parse failed) — verify before citing by name. ReActor also reports NO quantitative style/intent metric, only bounded parameterization as a qualitative safeguard.

findings.claim: OmniTrack produces physics-consistent references via policy rollouts, constituting prior art for execution-grounded reference correction
findings.evidence: arXiv:2602.23832. Abstract verbatim: 'In the first stage, a privileged generalist policy generates physically plausible motions that strictly adhere to the robot's dynamics via trajectory rollout in simulation. In the second stage, the general control policy is trained to track these physically feasible motions'. Rollouts stored as new references (joint states, global states, velocities, orientations, contacts); tracker trained with PPO plus deployment noise and domain randomization. Generalization claim is to 'unseen motions'. Real-world: hour-long stable tracking, flips, cartwheels, teleoperation. No intent/semantic preservation metric.
findings.consequence: Owns 'replace the flawed reference with what the robot actually did'. Structurally the anti-transfer case: the correction is not a model, it is a per-robot rollout artifact produced by that robot's own privileged policy, so there is nothing to move to a new robot. Use it as the argument that the field's current answer to reference artifacts is inherently non-amortizing. Its unmeasured semantic drift (the tracker is rewarded for following what the robot can do, not what the human meant) is a real, citable weakness that your intent-preservation conjunct exploits.

findings.claim: GenTrack alternates execution-grounded generator alignment with tracker training, and already measures intent preservation
findings.evidence: arXiv:2608.01410v2. Loop: FlowGRPO group-relative alignment of a text-conditioned generator, scored by rollout of a LAGGED tracker, dense reward (1-c) + [e_j]_2 + [e_t/0.5]_2 + 0.5[e_d/0.5]_2 + 2*I_fall; tracker retrained on equal parts public references and accepted generated motions; KL anchor to frozen init plus supervised rehearsal. Robot: 'All experiments use Unitree G1.' Splits: LAFAN1-G1, AMASS-test-G1, Wild-G1-clean (1,024 prompt-motion pairs). SONIC SR 85.0/79.0/47.2 -> 90.0/79.7/48.0; MPJPE 126.2 -> 124.1mm. Intent: TMR-G1 R@1/2/3 0.783/0.890/0.930, FID 0.020, and explicitly 'TMR-G1 retrieval and diversity are held-out metrics and do not enter the reward.' Critically: 'One-time offline GMD retargeting supplies paired initialization data, but no retargeter runs inside the online loop.'
findings.consequence: The closest prior work to your intent-preservation conjunct, and it sets the bar: semantic metrics held OUT of the reward so executability cannot be bought with semantic collapse. Copy that discipline exactly. Your defensible separation is narrow but real: GenTrack aligns a text-to-motion GENERATOR (no human source motion exists, so 'preserving human intent' is not even well-posed — it preserves text-prompt adherence), whereas you correct a retargeting of a specific human trajectory. State that distinction explicitly in the related-work paragraph or a reviewer will collapse the two.

findings.claim: AdaMorph's learned robot prompts and embodiment-specific adapters constitute prior art for robot-specification conditioning that transfers to new robots
findings.evidence: arXiv:2601.07284. Architecture: per-robot prompt bank P_r^(k) in R^(L_p x d_model) via cross-attention plus AdaLN modulation from Mean(P_r^(k)); embodiment-specific MLP heads psi_k projecting to R^(9+N_k) where N_k is that robot's motor count. Experiments: 'We retained 12 robots for training and evaluation, excluding 4 models where physically valid kinematic solutions could not be reliably converged upon by the retargeting optimizer.' Named: Unitree G1, H1, Hightorque Hi, Kuavo S45, Booster T1. Zero-shot section tests unseen MOTIONS: 'We curated a specific hold-out test set consisting of distinct stylized ethnic dance performances...strictly excluded from the training corpus.' No RL policy trained; MuJoCo used only for post-hoc visualization. Future work: 'extending this framework to physics-based control for robust sim-to-real transfer.'
findings.consequence: This is the single most important finding for your positioning. AdaMorph is the paper a reviewer will wave at you, and it does NOT do what its framing implies: all 12 robots are in training, zero-shot means unseen motions, and the conditioning is a LEARNED PER-ROBOT EMBEDDING plus a LEARNED PER-ROBOT OUTPUT HEAD — an unseen robot has neither, so the architecture cannot even be evaluated held-out without training new parameters. Your wedge is precise and defensible: condition on the ROBOT SPECIFICATION (URDF-derived kinematics, joint limits, link lengths, mass/inertia) rather than on a learned robot ID, which is the only conditioning that admits a held-out robot. Make this the architectural argument, not a benchmark argument. Also note AdaMorph has no physics and no downstream RL at all.

findings.claim: G-DReaM's graph conditioning already provides adaptation to new embodiments
findings.evidence: arXiv:2505.20857. Graph: node attribute = 3D unit joint rotation axis, edge attribute = parent->child vector with norm = link length, connectivity matrix in {0,1,2,3}; joint limits NOT encoded. Training with motion data: Unitree G1, H1, Tron1. Skeleton-only conditioning: Limx CL, Atlas, Talos, Cassie, Valkyrie. Adaptation, verbatim: 'We incorporate the skeleton data of the Valkyrie and Talos robots as desired graphs into our original training dataset, then the pretrained model is further trained using the expanded dataset' — ~30,000 steps, ~5 hours on RTX 4090. Limitations: generated motion 'violate[s] certain kinematic constraints, such as joint limits, foot-ground contact and collision avoidance'. No RL, no physics, no closed-loop feedback.
findings.consequence: Closest prior to genuine robot-specification conditioning: it encodes real morphology (link lengths, joint axes) rather than a robot ID, and it extends to embodiments with no motion data. But 'adaptation' is RETRAINING (~5h), not zero-shot inference, and it is purely kinematic with self-admitted joint-limit and contact violations, with zero downstream tracking evidence. This gives you two things: (a) precedent that spec-graph conditioning is the right representation, so you are not inventing it and should not claim it; (b) a compute-matched baseline you must beat — fine-tune G-DReaM-style on the held-out robot's skeleton for 5 GPU-hours and show your zero-shot correction matches or beats it.

findings.claim: KDMR enforces dynamics/contact constraints in retargeting and shows downstream benefit
findings.evidence: arXiv:2603.09956, 'Kinodynamic Motion Retargeting for Humanoid Locomotion via Multi-Contact Whole-Body Trajectory Optimization', Xiaoyu Zhang, Steven Haener, Varun Madabushi, Maegan Tucker. Abstract verbatim: 'KDMR extends beyond pure kinematics by explicitly enforcing rigid-body dynamics and contact complementarity constraints. Further, by integrating ground reaction force (GRF) measurements alongside MoCap data, our method automatically detects heel-toe contact events... We evaluate KDMR against the state-of-the-art baseline, GMR, across three key dimensions: 1) the dynamic feasibility and smoothness of the retargeted motions, 2) the accuracy of GRF tracking compared to raw source data, and 3) the training efficiency and final performance of downstream control policies trained via the BeyondMimic framework... yielding dynamically viable reference trajectories that accelerate policy convergence and enhance overall locomotion stability.'
findings.consequence: Independently confirms that 'dynamics-aware retargeting accelerates downstream policy convergence' is a settled, published claim — the fourth conjunct is worthless alone. Note it is pure trajectory optimization with no learned component, is locomotion-only, and needs a per-robot dynamics model plus GRF-instrumented capture. Its dependence on force-plate data is a scalability weakness you can contrast against, but do not claim the convergence-acceleration result itself as novel.

findings.claim: Advisor assertion: 'retargeting helps tracking', 'physics feedback', and 'shared morphology conditioning' are each individually insufficient novelty
findings.evidence: Retargeting-helps-tracking: owned by GMR (arXiv:2510.02252) as a controlled study, re-demonstrated by KDMR (2603.09956) and NMR (2603.22201). Physics feedback: owned by ReActor (2605.06593, bilevel RL-in-the-loop), OmniTrack (2602.23832, rollout-as-reference), GenTrack (2608.01410, execution-grounded GRPO), X-Morph (2606.30290, physics-aware correction). Morphology conditioning: owned by AdaMorph (2601.07284, 12 robots), G-DReaM (2505.20857, 8 embodiments), X-Morph (kinematic tree + joint limits + nominal base height metadata), and for policies H-Zero (2512.00971, embodiment descriptors incl. mass, inertia, joint limits).
findings.consequence: The advisor is right on all three, and understated the density: each conjunct has 3-4 owners, all from 2025-2026, several within the last six months. Any framing that leads with one of these will be desk-rejected as incremental.

findings.claim: Advisor's candidate conjunction — transferable correction learning + strict held-out-robot protocol + preserved human intent + downstream learning benefit — is unclaimed
findings.evidence: No work among the eight, nor among the near-misses found (X-Morph 2606.30290, OmniRetarget 2509.26633, Human2Humanoid 2606.03476, H-Zero 2512.00971), evaluates a retargeting correction on a held-out ROBOT. Closest per conjunct — transferable correction: AdaMorph (transfers only across TRAINED robots; per-robot prompt+head blocks unseen robots) and G-DReaM (extends to new skeleton but by ~5h retraining, physics-free). Held-out-robot protocol: H-Zero (train H1/N1/G1, test Adam/GR1/T1/PM01/OGHR/Kv/Atom/H1-2 + quadrupeds, zero-shot and 500-5k-epoch few-shot) — but locomotion policies, no human motion, no retargeting. Preserved human intent: GenTrack (TMR-G1 R-precision/FID held out of reward) — but for generated motion with no human source; ReActor claims 'characteristic motion' preservation with no quantitative metric. Downstream learning benefit: KDMR, NMR, GMR, ReActor — all single-robot, all seen-robot.
findings.consequence: The conjunction survives, but only as a conjunction, and the load is carried almost entirely by held-out-robot transfer — the other three conjuncts are borrowed protocol. This means the paper is a claim about TRANSFER, not a new method, and must be written that way. The strongest available framing is the negative space the literature itself marks: NMR's 'developing morphology-conditioned architectures remains a direction for future work' plus AdaMorph's structural inability to serve an unseen robot.

findings.claim: X-Morph is a sharper threat than any of the eight named works
findings.evidence: arXiv:2606.30290, 'X-Morph: Human Motion Priors for Scalable Robot Learning Across Morphologies', Sharma, Sood, Jain, Kesavamoorthi, He, Sartoretti (NUS). Conditions on morphology metadata: 'morphology by its kinematic tree and additional metadata such as joint limits, nominal base height, and feet or end-effectors'. Pipeline = morphology-aware retargeting -> physics-aware correction -> reference-conditioned closed-loop RL tracking with privileged teacher-student distillation. Robots: Go2 quadruped, Yuna hexapod, B2-Z1 quadruped-manipulator — trained per source-target pair, no held-out robot. Explicitly disclaims: 'we do not claim a sample-efficiency improvement over reinforcement learning from scratch, since a controlled baseline comparison is left for future work.'
findings.consequence: X-Morph already holds three of your four conjuncts (spec conditioning on real kinematic metadata, physics-aware correction, closed-loop tracking) on non-humanoid morphologies. It stops exactly at held-out-robot transfer and explicitly declines the downstream sample-efficiency claim. This makes your two remaining differentiators the entire paper — and makes it urgent that your sample-efficiency comparison is the controlled one X-Morph deferred, or you will be seen as taking the easy half of their future work. Cite it; do not let a reviewer find it first.

actions: Reframe the contribution from method to transfer claim. Do not lead with the architecture. Lead with: no existing retargeting-correction method can be evaluated on a robot it was not trained on — AdaMorph needs a new prompt bank and output head, G-DReaM needs ~5h retraining, ReActor needs ~6h of bilevel RL, OmniTrack needs that robot's own privileged policy, NMR states its pipeline is morphology-specific. Quote NMR's limitations sentence ('developing morphology-conditioned architectures remains a direction for future work', arXiv:2603.22201) in the introduction to establish the gap is literature-stated, not self-declared.

Make the conditioning architecturally spec-derived, not identity-derived, and say so as the technical argument. Condition on quantities readable from a URDF for any robot (link lengths, joint axes, joint limits, mass/inertia, kinematic tree topology, end-effector designation) with a shared output head over a canonicalized action space. The paper's defensibility rests on the claim that an unseen robot requires zero new parameters — verify this is literally true of your implementation before writing, because it is the one thing AdaMorph and X-Morph cannot say.

Run leave-one-robot-out (LORO) as the primary protocol, not an ablation. Train the correction model on N-1 humanoids, freeze, apply to the held-out robot with no gradient step and no re-optimization. Follow H-Zero (arXiv:2512.00971) in reporting a full LORO table rather than one favorable held-out robot, since with a small robot set a single held-out choice reads as cherry-picking.

Beat the compute-matched per-robot baselines on the held-out robot, or the paper fails. Required ladder: (a) GMR optimizer-only (arXiv:2510.02252) as the no-learning floor; (b) ReActor bilevel run on the held-out robot at its stated ~6 GPU-hours; (c) G-DReaM-style fine-tune with the new skeleton added, at its stated ~5 GPU-hours; (d) an AdaMorph-style per-robot prompt+head trained on held-out-robot data as the fit-it-directly upper bound. The claim that must survive is: equal or better than (b) and (c) at strictly lower compute on the new robot. Amortization, not accuracy, is the result.

Make the endpoint downstream tracker learning on the held-out robot, measured with an independent tracker. Use BeyondMimic exactly as GMR and KDMR did, and quote GMR's rationale ('does not depend on reward tuning and is developed independently from the retargeting methods') — this preempts the single most likely methodological attack, that gains came from reward engineering. Report both a sample-efficiency curve (episode length / success rate vs environment steps, as NMR Fig 4 and KDMR do) and final SR/MPJPE.

Adopt GenTrack's intent-metric discipline verbatim: measure semantic preservation with retrieval R@k and FID in a motion-text embedding space, and state explicitly that these metrics are HELD OUT of the training objective (GenTrack: 'TMR-G1 retrieval and diversity are held-out metrics and do not enter the reward'). Add an OmniRetarget-style contact/interaction-preservation check as the control against the degenerate solution of shrinking motion amplitude to buy executability.

Add the negative control that converts correlation to mechanism: condition on a shuffled or mismatched URDF specification at test time. If held-out-robot performance does not degrade, the conditioning is inert and the gains are just a better average retargeter — which is exactly what a hostile reviewer will allege. Run this before committing to the framing.

Add the scaling curve no per-robot method can produce: held-out-robot correction quality and downstream tracker sample-efficiency as a function of the number of training robots N. A positive slope is the one result that cannot be explained as a combination of AdaMorph and ReActor, and it upgrades the paper from 'conjunction' to 'phenomenon'. If the slope is flat, the transfer claim is not real and you should learn that early.

Cite X-Morph (arXiv:2606.30290) prominently and position against it explicitly. It already has spec conditioning + physics-aware correction + closed-loop tracking and explicitly defers the controlled sample-efficiency comparison. Your paper should be read as supplying that deferred comparison plus held-out-robot transfer, on humanoids. A reviewer who finds it before your related-work section will read the paper as taking the easy half of someone else's future work.

Verify two low-confidence details before citation: the second humanoid name in ReActor (rendered as 'Lima', ~0.84m/20 DoF; the PDF parse failed and only the HTML fetch reported it) and the full 12-robot list in AdaMorph (only G1, H1, Hightorque Hi, Kuavo S45, Booster T1 were named in the fetched text). Neither changes any conclusion here, but both would be embarrassing to misstate.
